planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in early spring in well-drained, mildly acidic soil sited in partial shade to protect the airy, upright form from wind damage; a second unrelated seedling nearby improves the fall berry display.

directions: Plant in well-drained, mildly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, giving the shrub room to develop its open, arching, vase-shaped habit rather than crowding it against other plantings. Tea viburnum is grown chiefly for its heavy fall display of long-lasting, translucent orange-red berries that dangle from the branches on drooping stalks well into winter, set off by narrow, willowy leaves that turn bronze-red before dropping. The common name comes from the historical use of dried young leaves as a tea substitute in parts of China, though it is grown ornamentally today. Because it flowers on old wood, prune only right after the spring bloom to avoid removing the berries that follow; light shade during the hottest afternoon hours helps keep foliage from scorching in warmer parts of its range.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in early spring in moist, well-drained loam in partial shade to full sun; plant two or more unrelated seedlings or cultivars nearby, since a single plant fruits poorly on its own.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained loam in partial shade to full sun; linden viburnum tolerates a wide range of soils and takes on some drought tolerance once its roots are established. The broad, felted, toothed leaves resemble those of a linden tree, giving the shrub its common name, and turn shades of russet and wine-red in autumn. Domed clusters of small white flowers open in late spring and are followed, on cross-pollinated plants, by a heavy fall crop of glossy red berries that persist into winter and draw overwintering songbirds. Its dense, rounded form and reliable fruit set make it a good understory screening shrub for a woodland edge or shaded property line.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; plant at least one male and one female close together, since this species is dioecious and only pollinated females produce the ornamental berries.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, though established plants tolerate deeper shade under high tree canopy. David viburnum is a low, mounded evergreen shrub from western China valued for its leathery, deeply three-veined, glossy dark green leaves that hold their color through winter, forming a dense architectural groundcover unlike most deciduous viburnums grown for flowers or fall color. Flattened heads of small white flowers appear in late spring, and where a male plant grows nearby, female shrubs set clusters of long-lasting, metallic turquoise-blue berries that are one of the more unusual fruit colors in the shade garden. Its tidy, spreading habit suits it to massing along a shaded foundation, edging a woodland path, or filling a bed beneath taller understory trees.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; site it near a path or entry where its winter fragrance can be enjoyed on mild days.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, in a sheltered spot away from harsh winter wind that can brown open flowers. 'Dawn' is an upright, multi-stemmed hybrid selected at Bodnant Garden in Wales, prized for clusters of small, tubular, rose-pink buds that open to pale pink and release a strong, sweet fragrance intermittently from late fall through late winter, often on bare wood well before other shrubs stir. The dull, coarsely toothed leaves emerge bronze-tinted in spring and take on modest red tones in fall, but the plant's main season of interest is the depth of winter, when little else in the shaded border is in bloom. Renewal-prune older stems back to the base every few years after flowering to keep the shrub from becoming leggy at its base.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained sandy soil in partial shade beneath high pine or hardwood canopy, mimicking the streamside pine-forest understory where this azalea naturally grows.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained sandy soil in partial shade, keeping roots consistently moist but never waterlogged. Texas azalea is a deciduous native shrub of the West Gulf Coastal Plain, found wild in sandy pine woods and along shaded stream banks of East Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma, where it forms a mounding, spreading thicket of slender branches. In mid-to-late spring, after or alongside the emerging leaves, clusters of narrow, glandular, white to pale pink tubular flowers open with a distinctive lemony-spice fragrance that carries well beyond the plant. Because it flowers later than many spring azaleas, it extends the native azalea bloom season in a partly shaded woodland border, and it is a useful nectar source for late-season pollinators including sphinx moths.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension (Texas Native Plants Database)

common_name: Semmes Beauty Oakleaf Hydrangea (Large-Panicle Native Oakleaf)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; allow 8-10 feet in all directions, since 'Semmes Beauty' is one of the larger oakleaf hydrangea selections.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun. 'Semmes Beauty' was selected in Alabama for its exceptionally long, dense flower panicles, which open pure white in early summer and gradually flush to a rich rose-pink as they age, held on strong stems that resist flopping even after summer rain. The large, deeply lobed, oak-shaped leaves are proportionally bold to match the flower size and turn shades of bronze, maroon, and burgundy in fall, while the shrub's peeling cinnamon bark adds interest through winter. Because it blooms on old wood, prune only immediately after flowering, and site it where its substantial mature size can be accommodated as a woodland-edge specimen or informal shaded screen.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in fall in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade; fresh seed sown as soon as ripe needs a period of cold, moist stratification and often takes a full year to germinate.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade, ideally on a gentle slope or in a woodland clearing where winter rain drains away from the crown. Green hellebore is a deciduous European species that dies back completely in summer and re-emerges in late winter with deeply divided, glossy leaves surrounding nodding clusters of flat, yellow-green flowers that open before most other perennials have stirred. Unlike the evergreen hybrid Lenten roses more commonly grown, its foliage disappears entirely after seed set, so it pairs well with later-emerging perennials or spring bulbs that can fill the gap it leaves in summer. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where pets or children graze on foliage, and handle divisions with gloves since the sap can irritate skin.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this deciduous species goes fully dormant in summer, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the crown.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; purple hellebore is a compact, deciduous Eastern European species grown for the unusual smoky, metallic purple tone of its cup-shaped, late-winter flowers, a color found in few other early-blooming shade perennials. Its deeply cut, palmate leaves emerge alongside or just after the flowers and provide a bold textural presence for the rest of the growing season before dying back completely by midsummer. Because the whole plant disappears in summer dormancy, it combines well with hostas, ferns, or later perennials that expand to cover the bare ground it leaves behind. Give it consistent moisture through spring while in active growth, tapering off as the foliage yellows and the plant enters dormancy.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in fall in moist, humus-rich, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade; this clump-forming, often evergreen hellebore resents root disturbance, so allow a full season to settle before dividing again.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees or in an open woodland margin. Fragrant hellebore is a clump-forming southeastern European species, often semi-evergreen where winters are mild, bearing outward-facing, saucer-shaped, apple- to yellow-green flowers from late winter into early spring that carry a soft, musky scent on some plants, though intensity varies from seedling to seedling. Its glossy, deeply divided foliage stays presentable for much of the year, giving structure to the shade border even when the plant is not in bloom. Site it where the flowers can be viewed from a slightly elevated angle or along a path edge, since the blooms tend to nod and face outward rather than fully upright.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins, or in early fall; plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade sheltered from harsh winter wind, which can damage the evergreen leaves.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Turkish epimedium is native to woodlands of the Balkans and Turkey and is among the tallest and most vigorous of the commonly grown epimedium species, forming a substantial evergreen clump of heart-shaped leaflets that emerge coppery-bronze before maturing to glossy dark green. In mid-spring, wiry stems carry open sprays of small, pale creamy-yellow flowers held well above the foliage, showier in quantity than in individual flower size. Once established, it tolerates dry shade under trees better than many perennials and needs little supplemental water beyond normal rainfall. Comb out or shear tattered old foliage in late winter before new leaves and flower stems emerge to keep the display clean.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in early spring or early fall; plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where this compact species spreads gradually to form a low, weed-suppressing edging.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; alpine barrenwort is a compact European species native to mountain woodlands of Italy and the western Balkans, valued as a low, long-lived edging or small-scale groundcover where taller epimediums would be out of scale. Wiry stems bear compound, heart-shaped leaflets on delicate stalks, and in spring carry loose racemes of small, unusual bicolor flowers with dull red sepals set off by contrasting yellow petals. It is one of the parent species behind many popular garden hybrid epimediums, but the true species itself remains an underused, tough, drought-tolerant choice for tucking along the front of a shaded bed or path. As with other epimediums, cut back old foliage in late winter so the modest flowers are not hidden.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; established clumps can be divided every few years in early spring to increase leaf-harvest plantings.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, watering during dry spells since this clumping woodland species does not tolerate drought. Gomchwi is a large-leaved perennial from the mountains of Korea, northern China, and the Russian Far East, prized in Korean cuisine as one of the most sought-after wild spring greens (sannamul); the young, mildly aromatic leaves are picked in early spring and eaten as a fresh wrap green, blanched, or preserved as pickled jangajji. Unlike its ornamental Ligularia relatives, it is grown primarily for repeated leaf harvest rather than for its tall late-summer spikes of yellow daisy-like flowers, though the flower stalks are also ornamental if left to bloom. Harvest outer leaves regularly through spring and early summer to encourage a continuous flush of tender new growth from the crown.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; shelter from strong wind, which can shred the large, soft leaflets.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade beside a pond, stream, or other reliably damp spot, since this rodgersia struggles wherever soil dries out for extended periods. Elderleaf rodgersia is a Chinese woodland species named for its pinnately compound leaves, which closely resemble those of an elderberry shrub rather than the palmately lobed foliage typical of most other rodgersia species, giving it a distinct, refined texture in the bog or shade garden. In midsummer, wiry flower stems rise well above the foliage mound carrying loose, feathery, creamy-white plumes reminiscent of a large astilbe. Mulch generously to retain soil moisture through summer, and divide congested clumps in early spring only when vigor declines, since rodgersias resent frequent disturbance.
